title: Let every spirit praise the Lord (Psalm 150)
hook: trumpets, harp, timbrel, cymbals, and everything that breathes

segments.voice: Yesterday, thou hast searched me: seen in every room, and still held. Your line was known, and not left. Who stayed? Today, the last psalm of all. Day one hundred ninety-one.

Trumpet. Psaltery and harp. Timbrel and choir. Strings and organs. High-sounding cymbals, then cymbals of joy. That's the last psalm in the book, and it reads like a finale, every player coming in at once and nobody holding anything back for later. The book of Psalms carries joy and grief, anger and trust. It ends here: every instrument sounding, and then the music handed to anyone with breath in their lungs. Today's word is the one it's built on: Alleluia.
screen: `THE LAST PSALM: A FINALE.` → `EVERY INSTRUMENT AT ONCE.` → `THEN, EVERYONE WHO BREATHES.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Alleluia is Hebrew, hallelu-Yah: hallelu, all of you, praise, and Yah, a short form of God's name. So it isn't a feeling, it's an invitation: everybody, praise God. It came into Greek and Latin untranslated, and Catholics still sing it that way today. Second, the orchestra. Psalm 150 is six verses and almost every line is a call to praise. It moves out from the sanctuary to the sky, then through the band. In the Douay-Rheims: "Praise him with sound of trumpet: praise him with psaltery and harp." Then timbrel and choir, strings and organs, and two kinds of cymbals. Nothing is held back. Third, the last line. After all the instruments, it lands on the one instrument everybody has. "Let every spirit praise the Lord. Alleluia." The Hebrew says everything that has breath. The Latin, and the Douay after it, say spirit. You don't need a trumpet. You need lungs. Fourth, how Catholics keep this word. The Alleluia is sung before the Gospel at Mass. But through the whole of Lent, the Church goes without it. On Easter night, at the Vigil, it comes back, sung three times, rising each time. So this is the end of our Psalms. Over thirty-five days we walked from the two ways of Psalm one, through the shepherd, the Miserere, the pilgrims' road, the depths and the rivers of exile, to a finale where everything that breathes is invited to join.
screen: `HALLELU-YAH: EVERYBODY, PRAISE GOD.` · `TRUMPET, HARP, TIMBREL, CYMBALS.` · `THE LAST INSTRUMENT: BREATH.` · `SILENT IN LENT, BACK AT EASTER.` · then, large: `LET EVERY SPIRIT PRAISE THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a slow alleluia. Settle, and breathe. Notice your breath going in and out on its own, without you asking. Now, on one long out-breath, let the word ride out quietly: al-le-lu-ia. Then just breathe for a while, and do it again when you're ready. If you pray, it's praise. If you don't, it's simply a long, slow breath out, noticing that you're alive. The bell holds the time.
Alleluia. From the Hebrew hallelu-Yah: all of you, praise God. The word the Psalms end on. Today's word.

Your line: everything that breathes. Today, notice one living thing breathing, a dog asleep, a baby, a bird, the person next to you, and count it in the choir. Tomorrow we open a gospel and read it straight through. Day one hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Catholics sing the Alleluia before the Gospel at Mass, omit it through Lent, and bring it back at the Easter Vigil; Psalm 150 is prayed at Morning Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours.

Part close: this is the last day of Part 1 (The Psalms, days 157–191); the teach looks back across it (Psalm 1 day 158, the shepherd day 163, the Miserere day 171, the gradual psalms day 184, De profundis day 187, Babylon day 189). 'Over thirty-five days' counts 157–191 inclusive.
Hebrew neshamah (breath) vs. Latin spiritus: 'breath and spirit are linked words in both languages' refers to spiritus (from spirare, to breathe) and ruach/neshamah. Confirm phrasing.
The Easter Vigil Alleluia intoned three times, each at a higher pitch: confirm rubric wording.
Psalm 150 at Morning Prayer (Sunday Week II / Week IV) in the Liturgy of the Hours; confirm.
Reviewer pass: 'goes without it for forty days' changed to 'through the whole of Lent', since the Alleluia is omitted from Ash Wednesday to the Easter Vigil, longer than forty days.

Editor review (days 189–206): new hook (was the banned 'Think of the end of a great concert'), built from the Douay's own instrument list (150:3–5: timbrel and choir, strings and organs, high-sounding cymbals, cymbals of joy) instead of KJV-style 'dancing, pipes, loud cymbals'; cut the superlative 'the most joyful noise in the Bible' and the breath/spirit etymology claim.
